A: What did you find in the museum? B: An old clock that belonged to my grandfather. A: Does it still work? B: Yes, but it is very noisy. Our family uses digital clocks now, while he still enjoys winding the old one.

A: Why did people need a lantern in the past? B: Some homes did not have electric lights. A: Do you still use one? B: Only when we go camping. My grandfather says he used to carry one outside after sunset.

listening2.passage:
Interviewer: Welcome to History at Home. Today we are talking to Grandmother Fatma. How did you keep in touch with friends when you were young?
Fatma: I wrote letters, and sometimes we used the telephone at the post office. We did not have mobile phones.
Interviewer: Did you have a computer at school?
Fatma: No. Our teachers wrote on the board, and we used notebooks. We learned a lot, but finding information took longer.
Interviewer: What did you do for entertainment?
Fatma: We visited neighbours, told stories and played outside. My brothers made toys from simple materials.
Interviewer: Could you take photographs easily?
Fatma: My father had an old camera, but we saved film for special days. We could not see a photograph straight away.
Interviewer: What is better today?
Fatma: We can communicate quickly and learn about the world. However, I think families should still spend time speaking together.
Interviewer: Thank you for sharing your memories.
Fatma: It was a pleasure.

reading2.passage:
When Yaqoub visited his grandfather's house, he found an old box full of letters and photographs. His grandfather explained that people had kept important memories in boxes before computers became common. One letter was from a friend who had moved to another town many years earlier.

Yaqoub was surprised that the letter had taken several days to arrive. He could send a message on his tablet in only a few seconds. His grandfather smiled and said that writing a letter could still be special because people chose their words carefully.

Later, they looked at a photograph of Yaqoub's father as a child. He was standing beside a small bicycle. At that time, he could not ride it without help, but now he often cycled with his children. Yaqoub decided to scan the photograph so the family could keep another copy. His grandfather was pleased that old memories could be shared using new technology.
